solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: What'll we see serge in? Our recommendation has mark of correctness

parts.note: Azed recommends the Chambers Dictionary to his solvers, so 'our recommendation' is CHAMBERS
a tick is the mark a teacher puts beside a right answer

explanation.surface: A tailor wonders where to view serge cloth and is pointed to a recommended source with a seal of approval.
explanation.walkthrough: Serge here is not the cloth: Chambers lists SERGE (also CERGE, CIERGE) as a large wax candle, and a chamberstick is a candleholder you carry to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A chamberstick is a short candlestick with a handle, the holder in which a candle would be seen.

clue.text: School's dep. sacked where union holds sway (10, two words)

indicators.note: a place that is sacked is ransacked and turned upside down, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A school's department has been dismissed in a workplace run by the union.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sacked' signals the rearrangement; 'dep.' is an abbreviation for department, but its letters are used as written: SCHOOLSDEP.
explanation.definitionFit: A closed shop is a workplace where all employees must belong to a trade union, so the union has control.

clue.text: Like beefcake in thick pieces without cold topping

indicators.note: 'without' says the letter for cold is removed from the word
'topping' says it is the top letter that goes, the first in a down entry

parts.note: chunky means in thick lumps or pieces
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: A description of a chunky meat dish served without any cold garnish on top.
explanation.walkthrough: Beefcake is slang for muscular, attractive men. 'without cold topping' takes the C off the top of CHUNKY, the front in a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Hunky means ruggedly handsome and muscular, the look that beefcake photographs show off.

clue.text: Member of sect? I'll get involved in second one

parts.note: MO is short for moment, a second

indicators.note: 'get involved in' puts the letter inside the word one

parts.note: taken as written
the letter I, the 'll being the auxiliary verb of the sentence

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether they will be drawn into a sect in a moment.
explanation.walkthrough: MO is a moment ('half a mo'); 'get involved in' puts I into ONE to make ONIE.
explanation.definitionFit: A Moonie is a follower of Sun Myung Moon's Unification Church, so one belonging to a religious sect.

clue.text: Book penned in a thorny tree? An ill- conceived idea

indicators.note: 'penned in' says the letter for book is enclosed by the tree

parts.note: the bael is a thorny Indian tree, the Bengal quince

explanation.surface: A book kept in a thorny tree sounds like a bad plan.
explanation.walkthrough: The bael is the Bengal quince of India, a spiny tree grown for its fruit; 'penned in' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Babel, after the tower, means a confused scheme or a visionary plan that cannot work, as Chambers gives.

clue.text: Hut for travellers rest, last given precedence

indicators.note: the last letter is allowed to go first, moved to the front of the word

parts.note: an anchor is a rest or support, as in anchorage

explanation.surface: A hut where travellers rest, the last to arrive being given priority.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last given precedence' takes the R from the end of ANCHOR and puts it at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: In Chambers, rancho is a hut or group of huts for housing travellers in Spanish America.

clue.text: Jock's rattled, with bonds round both hands

definitions.note: past tense verb: Scots tirl means to rattle

indicators.note: 'round' puts the tied word around the two hand letters

parts.note: tied means bound, fastened with bonds
R and L, right and left, are the two hands

explanation.surface: A Scotsman shaken up after being bound hand and foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jock' marks a Scots word: to tirl is to rattle, as at a door-latch. 'round' is the container signal; right and left are the two hands.
explanation.definitionFit: Tirled is Scots for rattled or twirled, especially a door-pin rattled to ask for entry.

clue.text: Having completed MA, I had about abandoned pen etc

indicators.note: 'about' places the contraction around the rearranged letters

parts.note: I'd is the contraction of I had

indicators.note: something done in an abandoned way is wild and unrestrained, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A graduate who has finished an MA throws away pens and stationery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abandoned' scrambles PEN ETC to NCEPTE and 'about' wraps the contraction of I had round it. At Cambridge, to incept was to take a master's or doctor's degree, so 'MA' belongs to the definition, not the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To incept, in the old university sense, is to be admitted to a master's degree, so incepted means having qualified.

clue.text: Devilish villainess gang once completely overturned

parts.note: crue is an obsolete spelling of crew, a gang

indicators.note: 'overturned' says the word for completely is turned the other way round

parts.note: all means wholly, completely

explanation.surface: A wicked woman whose old gang was totally defeated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Devilish' hints at her surname, de Vil. 'gang once' signals an archaic spelling of crew, and 'overturned' applies only to the word for completely, making LLA.
explanation.definitionFit: Cruella de Vil is the fur-loving villain of The Hundred and One Dalmatians.

clue.text: Ivy follows line that's contested on the board

indicators.note: 'follows' puts the plant's name after the single letter for line

parts.note: udo is a Japanese plant of the ivy family, Araliaceae

explanation.surface: Ivy creeps along a line drawn on some disputed board.
explanation.walkthrough: UDO (Aralia cordata) belongs to the ivy family, which lets Azed call it 'Ivy'; it 'follows' L.
explanation.definitionFit: Ludo is a board game, so it is played out, or contested, on a board.

clue.text: Some banks charging extras? A racket

definitions.note: plural noun: asar are glacial ridges or banks

indicators.note: a gun charging its load holds it inside, so the phrase holds the answer within its letters

parts.note: the answer is held across the end of extras, the word A and the start of racket

explanation.surface: A complaint that some banks levy extra fees, which is a racket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charging' (loading, holding) signals the answer carried inside extrAS A Racket. ASAR is the plural of OS, an esker: a long ridge of gravel left by a glacier.
explanation.definitionFit: Asar are long gravel ridges, a kind of natural bank, so a few of them are some banks.

clue.text: Southern borough the Scots plundered

parts.note: a borough is a town

explanation.surface: Raiders from Scotland sack a southern English town.
explanation.walkthrough: Stown is a Scots past participle of steal.
explanation.definitionFit: Stown is the Scots form of stolen, and something stolen in a raid has been plundered.

clue.text: What Japanese rarely dressed without — or is this for ferry?

indicators.note: says the clue word stands, in the ferry's name, for the start of this answer, so swapping back gives the answer

parts.note: a ro-ro is a roll-on roll-off ferry
the word 'or' read from the back gives the pair of letters standing in the ferry's opening

explanation.surface: A puzzled note about Japanese dress, then a sudden question about a ferry.
explanation.walkthrough: Write RORO, the ferry; its first RO is 'or' reversed, and 'is this for' says that stands in for this answer's IN. Put IN back in its place.
explanation.definitionFit: An inro is a small lacquered box hung from the sash of traditional Japanese dress, so it was rarely left off.

clue.text: Unwelcome comforters called this 'doing normal work'

definitions.meaning: Job's comforters, who made his suffering worse
... means happening during one's usual work, as in ... training

explanation.walkthrough: Job's comforters are proverbial friends whose sympathy only adds to the misery; in the Book of Job they come and call on him.
explanation.definitionFit: On-job describes something done at the workplace as part of everyday duties, the same idea as on-the-job.

clue.text: Ocular deposit? Old poet, I'll be seen with this, possibly

definitions.meaning: a ring of fatty deposit round the cornea of the eye

definitions.text: Old poet, I'll be seen with this, possibly
definitions.meaning: ... senilis, the form seen in elderly eyes, so an old poet might be seen with it

explanation.walkthrough: The full term is arcus senilis, a pale ring round the iris common in old age, which is why an old poet might have it.
explanation.definitionFit: The arcus is a grey or white ring of lipid laid down in the cornea, a deposit in the eye.

clue.text: Peg ropes on board ship, showing stamina

indicators.note: 'on board' puts the peg and ropes inside the ship's letters

parts.note: SS is the abbreviation for steamship
a tee is the peg a golf ball sits on
lines are ropes on a ship

explanation.surface: A sailor stows pegs and ropes aboard ship and shows great endurance.
explanation.definitionFit: Steeliness is hardness of character, a toughness like steel, so the staying power of stamina.

clue.text: Knife, even used in cracking cockles

indicators.note: 'used in' sets the word for even inside the scrambled shellfish
cockles cracked open are broken up, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: ENE is an old and dialect form of even, meaning evening

explanation.surface: A knife is used in the evening to crack open cockles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cracking' scrambles COCKLES to SKOCCLE and 'used in' puts the old word for evening inside. Skene-occle is a variant of sgian-dubh, the knife a Highlander tucks in a stocking.
explanation.definitionFit: A skene-occle is a Highland dagger carried in the sleeve or stocking, a type of small blade.

clue.text: Pay o? bit left in a payment due to new ruler

indicators.note: 'in' puts the scrap inside the payment

parts.note: a mise was a payment made to a new king or lord on his accession
an ort is a scrap of food left over

explanation.surface: Settle a debt by paying a leftover amount to a new monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is 'Pay off'; the double f was lost in the copy. A mise was an old feudal payment to a new king or lord; 'in' puts the scrap inside, making MORTISE.
explanation.definitionFit: To amortise a debt is to pay it off gradually by instalments.

clue.text: Scots pipe was reeling, mostly round piano

definitions.note: verb: to pipe is to whistle

indicators.note: 'round' puts the shortened word around the musical letter
'mostly' says to drop the word's final letter

parts.note: something that was reeling wheeled round
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, soft

explanation.surface: A Scots bagpipe tune was spinning dizzily around a piano.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' cuts WHEELED to WHEELE, and 'round' wraps that around P. To wheeple in Scots is to whistle feebly, as a curlew does.
explanation.definitionFit: Wheeple is a Scots verb meaning to whistle weakly, and pipe also means to whistle shrilly.

clue.text: Behaviour of Trump men adore, abnormally

definitions.note: Trump points to the American spelling of demeanour

indicators.note: letters arranged abnormally are put in an unusual order

explanation.surface: A wry look at how Donald Trump behaves, and how his followers adore him beyond reason.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abnormally' rearranges MEN ADORE; 'of Trump' signals the US spelling without the U, which is why eight letters are enough.
explanation.definitionFit: Demeanor is the way a person conducts or presents themselves, their outward manner; this is the American spelling.

clue.text: Norman going after English? He sends unwritten message

indicators.note: 'going after' puts the novelist's surname after the letter for English

parts.note: Norman Mailer, the American novelist

explanation.surface: Norman Mailer chasing an English rival who sends spoken messages.
explanation.walkthrough: Mailer wrote The Naked and the Dead and is 'going after' E. An email is typed, not handwritten, hence 'unwritten'.
explanation.definitionFit: An emailer is one who sends electronic mail, a message never put down on paper.

clue.text: Drink up, a drink (not grand) imbibed? They could be grand

indicators.note: 'imbibed' says the article and shortened drink are taken inside the reversed word
'up' in a down clue says the word is read from the bottom upwards, backwards

parts.note: to sip is to drink

indicators.note: 'not grand' says the letter for grand is dropped

parts.note: nog is a strong ale, or eggnog
G is the abbreviation for grand, a thousand

explanation.surface: Drink up, have a drink but not a big one, then wonder about pianos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses the first drink to PIS, 'not' grand drops G from the second to leave NO, and 'imbibed' puts A NO inside. The final 'grand' is the definition's, a different sense from the G.
explanation.definitionFit: Pianos come in grand and upright forms, so some of them may be grands.

clue.text: What, digging into pot, my very tight clothes do, bit by bit

parts.words: What, digging into pot, my very tight clothes do
parts.note: set the answer inside POT and it reads PINCH ME A LOT, which is what very tight clothes do

explanation.surface: Someone complains that their snug clothes keep nipping them as they eat.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue describes the result of putting the answer into POT: P-INCHMEAL-OT, read as 'pinch me a lot'.
explanation.definitionFit: Inchmeal is an old adverb meaning gradually, by small degrees, an inch at a time.

clue.text: Write a score part for one of the foregoing? Ta — terriffc

indicators.note: only part of the run of words is wanted, so the letters either side of the answer are dropped

parts.note: the clue before this one gives pianos, so one of the foregoing is a piano
terrific, misspelt in this copy of the clue

explanation.surface: A grateful composer thanks someone for a terrific arrangement.
explanation.walkthrough: This clue leans on the previous one: 21 down is PIANOS, so 'one of the foregoing' is PIANO. Write PIANO TA TERRIFIC and take 'part' of it: dropping PIA leaves NOTATERRIFIC, and dropping RRIFIC leaves the answer. 'terriffc' is a slip for terrific.
explanation.definitionFit: To notate music is to write it down in notation, as a composer writes a score.

clue.text: Part of marine organism, catch hauled up devoured by odd members of crew

indicators.note: 'devoured by' says the reversed word is swallowed inside the two letters
the first and third letters, the odd-numbered ones

parts.note: taken as written; its odd letters are taken

indicators.note: in a down clue, hauled up means read upwards, backwards

parts.note: to net is to catch

explanation.surface: A fishing net is pulled up and its catch eaten by some of the crew.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odd members of' takes letters one and three of crew, CE. In a down clue 'hauled up' means read upwards, giving TEN, and 'devoured by' has the pair swallow it. The organism is a comb jelly, not a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A ctene is one of the comb-like swimming plates of a comb jelly, part of that sea creature.

clue.text: Half of Panama let off It's to do with canal's opening

definitions.text: It's to do with canal's opening

indicators.note: 'off' as in gone off, spoiled, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: the last three of Panama's six letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: Half of Panama is allowed off work, a matter about the canal's opening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' rearranges AMA and LET. The canal is not the Panama Canal but an anatomical one: meatal relates to a meatus, the opening of a bodily passage.
explanation.definitionFit: Meatal is the adjective for meatus, the opening of a passage in the body, such as the ear canal.

clue.text: A grain, mostly included in heated meat stew with veg, …

indicators.note: 'included in' puts the article and the shortened grain inside the word for heated

parts.note: heated means hot

indicators.note: 'mostly' says to drop the final letter of the grain

parts.note: rice is a cereal grain

explanation.surface: A recipe step: add some grain to a hot stew of meat and vegetables, with more to follow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' trims the grain to RIC and 'included in' puts A plus that inside the word for heated. The ellipsis runs on to the next clue, the pudding after this course.
explanation.definitionFit: A haricot is a ragout, especially of mutton, cooked with beans or turnips, so a meat-and-vegetable dish.

clue.text: Had onset of niggle in insides, laid up

definitions.note: past participle: had means cheated, as in 'you've been had'

indicators.note: laid up in a down clue reads as lifted upwards, so read backwards
'in' puts that letter inside the word for insides

parts.note: guts are the insides

indicators.note: 'onset of' picks the opening letter of niggle

parts.note: its first letter is used

explanation.surface: A patient who had stomach twinges is now confined to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'onset of' niggle gives N; 'in' puts it inside GUTS to make GNUTS, and 'laid up' turns that upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Stung, in slang, means swindled or overcharged, the same as being had.

clue.text: Topper collapsing, second in line, with nasty bugs around

indicators.note: 'around' puts the rearranged insects around that letter
something nasty is messed up, so the letters are put in disorder

parts.note: the second letter of line

explanation.surface: A top hat falls apart; next in queue, horrible insects swarm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nasty' scrambles BUGS to GBUS, and 'around' puts that about I, line's second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A gibus is an opera hat, a top hat with a spring that lets it fold flat.

clue.text: … Followed by this treat cooked by Jacques, new? (10, two words)

definitions.note: the dessert served after the stew of the previous clue

indicators.note: 'by' sets the comedian's surname beside the rearranged word
a treat that is cooked is reworked, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: Jacques Tati was the French film-maker behind Monsieur Hulot

explanation.surface: The stew is to be followed by a dessert made by a Frenchman named Jacques.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooked' makes TARTE out of TREAT. The clue continues the previous one: a haricot (stew) followed by this pudding.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarte Tatin is an upside-down caramelised apple tart, a natural course to come after a main dish.

clue.text: Pizzicato sound, soft, part of chain

parts.note: P, piano, is the musical abbreviation for soft
a link is one ring of a chain

explanation.surface: A quiet plucked note likened to one link in a chain of sounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A plink is a short light ringing note, the kind made by plucking a string.

clue.text: Basin replacing bend in use for piping that's far from straight

indicators.note: 'replacing' says the basin word takes the place of the bend letter

parts.note: taken as written
S is the shape of a double bend, as on road signs
a tub is a basin or open vessel

explanation.surface: Advice to a plumber on swapping a basin and bending pipes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'replacing' swaps TUB for the S in USE.
explanation.definitionFit: A U-tube is a pipe bent into the shape of a U, a length of tubing with a sharp curve.

clue.text: Monetary unit in Peru and so on

parts.note: PE is the international code for Peru
taken as written

explanation.surface: A query about the currency of Peru and similar countries.
explanation.walkthrough: Peru itself uses the sol, not the peso, which is part of the misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: The peso is the currency of Mexico, Chile, Colombia and others, a unit of money.

clue.text: US secretary with no love for deadly piece

indicators.note: 'with no' says the letter for love is taken away

parts.note: steno is American for a stenographer, a shorthand secretary
love is zero in tennis, so O

explanation.surface: An American secretary with no love life looks for a lethal weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sten was a British submachine gun of the Second World War; piece is slang for a firearm.

clue.text: Mean muse that's shunned this writer twice — waste passage ends here

indicators.note: 'that's shunned' says those pronouns are kept out of the two words

parts.note: taken as written
this writer is ME, the setter; twice gives two of them
taken as written

explanation.surface: A spiteful muse has turned her back on the poet, and his work ends in the bin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'this writer' is the setter, ME, and 'that's shunned' takes him out of both words, 'twice': MEAN leaves AN, and MUSE, losing M then E (via USE), leaves US.
explanation.definitionFit: The anus is the opening at the end of the digestive tract, where waste leaves the body.

clue.text: Urged girl to accept good moulded fragile stuff (12, two words)

indicators.note: 'to accept' says the urged girl takes in the letter for good, between the two words

parts.note: to press someone is to urge them
lass is a girl

explanation.surface: Someone pressed a girl to take some delicate ornament as a gift.
explanation.walkthrough: The container is the whole of 'Urged girl', so 'to accept' sets the letter for good at the join between the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Pressed glass is glass shaped in a mould under pressure, breakable material formed that way.
